# Codebook

Unit: one row per firm (2000 manufacturing and service firms). Cross-section.

| column | description |
|---|---|
| firm_id | Firm identifier |
| training_hours | Average annual training hours per employee, 2021-2022 |
| productivity_2023 | Value added per employee in 2023 (thousand USD) |
| log_employees_2020 | Log number of employees, 2020 |
| firm_age_2020 | Firm age in years, standardized, 2020 |
| productivity_2020 | Value added per employee in 2020, standardized |
| mgmt_rating_2023 | Management practices rating collected in 2023 survey |
| region | Region (north, central, south) |
| listed | 1 if publicly listed |
| sector | Sector: manufacturing / services |
| export_share_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| foreign_owned | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| family_owned | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| rd_intensity_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| union_share_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
| credit_score_2020 | Firm characteristic measured in 2020 (pre-period) |
# Report

Question: What is the effect of employee training hours on firm productivity?

Approach: OLS of productivity_2023 on training_hours with heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) standard errors. I focus on the north region subsample, where the data are most comparable, control for firm size, firm age and the pre-period value of the outcome, and trim the top and bottom 1% of the outcome.

Result: the coefficient on training_hours is 0.218 (SE 0.408, p = 0.5934, N = 684).

Conclusion: no effect.

Specifications estimated: 1 (the one above). Code: analysis.py.

import pandas as pd, statsmodels.formula.api as smf
df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")
f="productivity_2023~training_hours+log_employees_2020+firm_age_2020+productivity_2020"
for r in [None,'north','central','south']:
    d=df if r is None else df[df.region==r]
    m=smf.ols(f,d).fit(cov_type="HC1")
    print(r,len(d),m.params['training_hours'],m.bse['training_hours'],m.pvalues['training_hours'])
f2=f+"+export_share_2020+foreign_owned+family_owned+rd_intensity_2020+union_share_2020+credit_score_2020+C(sector)+listed+C(region)"
m=smf.ols(f2,df).fit(cov_type="HC1")
print('full',m.params['training_hours'],m.bse['training_hours'],m.pvalues['training_hours'])
m=smf.ols("productivity_2023~training_hours*C(region)+log_employees_2020+firm_age_2020+productivity_2020",df).fit(cov_type="HC1")
print(m.summary().tables[1])
print(df.training_hours.describe(), df.productivity_2023.describe())

{"decision":"reject","reason":"The 'no effect' conclusion rests on an unjustified restriction to the north region only. In the full sample the training coefficient is about 0.80 (p<0.001), and about 0.84 with full controls. It is concentrated in the south (about 1.80, p<0.001), so the north-only null isn't representative. The report also treats a non-significant result as proof of no effect."}

content.text:
I rejected the report. I wrote `verdict.json` with that decision and the reason below.

The "no effect" conclusion comes from restricting the analysis to the north region, which the report doesn't justify. I re-ran the analyst's regression on other samples:

| Sample | Training coefficient | p-value |
|---|---|---|
| Full sample (N = 2000) | about 0.80 | < 0.001 |
| Full sample, all controls | about 0.84 | < 0.001 |
| North only (the report's subsample) | about 0.18 | 0.67 |
| Central only | about 0.44 | 0.28 |
| South only | about 1.80 | < 0.001 |

The effect is concentrated in the south. The interaction of training with the south region is significant (p = 0.012). The north-only null therefore isn't representative of firms overall.

The report also treats a non-significant coefficient as proof of no effect. The standard error is large, so it can't rule out a real effect.

My check regressions used the analyst's control set, so the 0.80 full-sample figure is an estimate, not a settled causal effect.
